subject: What Changed to Your Credit Card Today? Edition 11
summary: Standard Chartered redesigned its card pages today, mostly noise, but the Ultimate Credit Card picked up a new 1% processing fee on rent payments, Manhattan's minimum age dropped to 18, and Super Value Titanium lost its specific income eligibility number.
body_html:
A quick note before we start: today's batch is messier than usual. Standard Chartered India redid its credit card pages across the board today, seven cards flagged as changed, and most of what moved is page-redesign noise: reworded boilerplate, HTML formatting cleanup, feature blurbs shuffled around. I dug through all seven and I'm only writing up what's actually real, fee changes, eligibility changes, and new benefit disclosures. If a card isn't mentioned below for something specific, assume what changed on its page today doesn't affect your money.

Two things showed up on more than one card, so let's flag those first, then go card by card for what's specific to each.

Portfolio-wide: a new "sourcing city" eligibility line. Standard Chartered added "Applicants should belong to credit card sourcing cities/locations of the Bank" to several card pages today (Super Value Titanium, Manhattan, Smart, and Rewards, among others). Standard Chartered has never issued cards everywhere in India, they've always sourced from a specific city list, but explicitly stating it on the page is new. If you're applying fresh from a city Standard Chartered doesn't source from, this is worth confirming with the bank directly before you apply, since it wasn't spelled out this plainly before.

Portfolio-wide: a processing fee billing-timing disclosure. DigiSmart, Super Value Titanium, and Ultimate all added a line saying processing fees "will be levied by the 15th of the next calendar month and will have a separate narration in the monthly statement." This doesn't create a new fee, it clarifies when an existing fee actually posts and how it'll be labelled, so it doesn't come as a surprise line item.

DigiSmart Credit Card

Beyond the portfolio-wide billing-timing note above, nothing material changed here today. The rest of the diff is HTML formatting cleanup on the page.

The catch: none, this one's a non-event beyond the billing clarification everyone else got too.

Super Value Titanium Credit Card

The specific minimum income requirement, "INR 55,000 per month," is gone from the eligibility section, replaced with the vaguer "Applicant should have a stable monthly income." That's not necessarily good news: a specific number tells you exactly where you stand, a vague standard leaves Standard Chartered more room to reject you subjectively even if you'd have cleared the old ₹55,000 bar.

I also want to flag something honestly rather than pretend I'm certain: the page's annual benefit value chart changed from a fuel-and-utility-focused illustration (totalling around ₹7,050 a year) to a generic online/offline spend chart totalling ₹18,000, the exact same chart that now also appears on the unrelated Smart Credit Card's page. That looks more like a page-template mix-up from today's redesign than a deliberate change to this card's actual cashback structure, since this card is positioned as a fuel card and the new chart doesn't mention fuel at all. I wouldn't treat ₹18,000 as this card's real annual value yet, I'd confirm the fuel cashback structure directly with Standard Chartered or on your card's actual terms document before relying on either number.

The 90,000 renewal fee waiver we flagged back on 25 August is still there, unchanged.

The catch: don't take the ₹18,000 value chart at face value for this specific card, it looks like a copy-paste artifact, and the loss of a hard income number in the eligibility section means you can't self-assess your odds as precisely as before.

Manhattan Credit Card

One genuine win here: the minimum eligible age dropped from 21 to 18 years. If you're an 18-to-20-year-old with a stable income, you can now apply for this card where you couldn't before.

The catch: none for existing holders, and it's a straightforward eligibility widening, not a downgrade, for new applicants.

Priority Visa Infinite Credit Card

The page now spells out benefit details that weren't clearly listed before: 5 reward points per ₹100 spent overseas or on retail fashion, 2 points per ₹100 on everything else, 4 complimentary domestic lounge visits per quarter, 2 international lounge visits a month via Priority Pass for FUM-qualified clients (FUM means Funds Under Management, the assets you hold with the bank), and complimentary overseas insurance: ₹1 crore air accident cover plus USD 25,000 medical cover.

I can't tell you with certainty whether these numbers are new benefits or just newly documented existing ones, Standard Chartered's page didn't carry this level of detail before today. Either way, if you hold this card, it's worth reading in full since it's more specific than what was public until now. One concrete addition: self-employed applicants now need to submit Latest IT Returns and Business Continuity proof as part of the application, a documentation requirement that wasn't listed before.

The catch: if you're a self-employed professional considering this card, budget time to pull together IT returns and business continuity proof before you apply, that's a real new step in the process.

Smart Credit Card

Nothing material changed on this card today beyond the portfolio-wide "sourcing city" eligibility line mentioned above. The rest of today's diff, including a reformatted version of the card's existing ₹18,000 annual cashback illustration, restates numbers that were already public, just in table form instead of a headline banner.

The catch: none.

Ultimate Credit Card

The real find in today's batch: a new 1% processing fee (plus taxes) on rental transactions made through third-party rent payment platforms using this card. Standard Chartered's own example: pay ₹20,000 in rent through a platform and you'll be charged roughly ₹200 plus taxes as a processing fee, billed by the 15th of the following month with its own line item on your statement.

If you pay ₹25,000 a month in rent on this card specifically to earn rewards, that's about ₹250 to ₹300 a month, ₹3,000 to ₹3,600 a year, in processing fees you weren't paying before, on top of whatever your rent platform itself charges. Weigh that against what you're actually earning in reward points on that rent spend, at this card's stated 5 points per ₹100 on eligible categories, before assuming rent-on-card is still worth it here.

On the upside, the page also added a genuinely useful new value chart specific to this card: 4 golf sessions worth ₹20,000, 6 domestic lounge visits worth ₹8,400, 4 global lounge visits with Priority Pass worth ₹9,200, duty-free cashback worth ₹2,000, foreign markup cashback worth ₹750, reward points worth up to ₹26,000, and joining-fee reward points worth ₹6,000, adding up to a stated ₹74,150 in annual benefit value against this card's ₹5,000 joining and renewal fees.

The catch: the new rent processing fee is real money if you were using this card for rent payments specifically to hit reward thresholds or milestones, do the math on your specific rent amount before your next payment cycle. The ₹74,150 value chart, unlike Super Value Titanium's, looks genuinely tied to this card's actual golf-and-lounge positioning, but remember it's an illustration assuming you use every single benefit, not a guaranteed number.

Rewards Credit Card

Nothing material beyond the portfolio-wide "sourcing city" eligibility addition. The annual fee (₹1,000 plus GST, reversed on ₹1,50,000 of spend in the previous year) and the reward point structure (4 points per ₹150 on retail, 1 point per ₹150 on government and insurance spends) are both unchanged, just re-formatted.

The catch: none.

What I'd actually do with this

If you're applying fresh for any Standard Chartered card and you're not sure whether your city is on their sourcing list, ask before you apply, don't assume you'll be approved just because you were eligible on paper before today.

If you hold the Ultimate Credit Card and use it for rent payments, run the actual numbers on your rent amount against the new 1% processing fee before your next cycle. It might still be worth it for the reward points, but don't assume it is without checking.

If you hold the Super Value Titanium, don't plan around the ₹18,000 value chart shown on the page right now, it looks like a template error borrowed from an unrelated card. Call Standard Chartered or check your card's actual terms document if you want the real number for this card's fuel cashback.

If you're 18 to 20 and were counting yourself out of the Manhattan Credit Card because of the old age floor, you're eligible now.

This is my honest read, not formal financial advice. I'm not your advisor, and before you make a call on any of this, run it past a professional or at least sleep on it. But this is exactly how I'd think about it if these were my cards.

Monzy
